paragraphs.text: Lesson 23, getting a raise.
Vance and Aaron are co-workers who have the same boss, Mr. Brown.
Listen to Aaron give Vance advice on getting a raise and answer the comprehension questions.
I really, really need a raise.
Melinda isn't saying it to my face, but she wants this house we looked at on Snowy Lane.
She knows we can't afford it unless I get a raise.
So talk to Mr. Brown and ask for one.
You've been with this company for a decade now, and you've got a great track record.
You're honest.
You put in overtime when needed.
You deserve a raise.
I know, I know.
It's just that Mr. Brown is always fussing about how we need to cut costs around here.
He's not exactly the type of boss it hands out raises like candy.
Mr. Brown definitely doesn't tolerate any nonsense, but sometimes that's for the best.
How so?
Mr. Brown respects men who are up front and straight forward.
He doesn't like weaklings.
If you go into his office hanging your head and beating around the bush, he's just going
to kick you out.
You have to march into that man's office with your chin up, look him in the eye, and ask
with confidence.
That's what I did.
And Mr. Brown gave you a raise?
Not right away.
At first he yelled at me and then he threw a lot of financial numbers around and so on.
But I held my ground.
My twins were about to go to college with a double tuition bill to boot.
So I let him know that unless I got a raise I would have to leave and find a job that would
support my family better.
I can't believe you pulled that off.
Look, Mr. Brown is in blind.
He knows the cost of living is going up.
He also knows we give it our all.
If you go in there asking for a raise to buy a new boat then you don't have a chance.
But if you explain that you want to buy a new home for your pregnant wife, I'm sure he'll
understand.
The apartment Melinda and I are living in is pretty small.
And when the baby arrives space will be very tight.
Then march into Mr. Brown's office and tell him just that.
I promise you, he's a reasonable man.
Sure he might bark at you.
But don't back down.
I hope I don't catch him on a bad day.
I can just picture getting fired with a baby on the way.
You're not going to get fired.
Now go see Mr. Brown before he leaves for the day.
Well, here goes.
Raise or no raise?
I have to try.
Melinda and the baby deserve it.
That's the spirit.
And don't be surprised if Mr. Brown melts a little and buys you a housewarming present.
Let's take a look at the vocabulary from this dialogue.
Vance's wife isn't saying it to his face, but she wants a certain house that they looked
at.
Saying it to someone's face means saying it directly to that person.
However, Vance and Melinda can't afford the house unless Vance gets a raise.
If you can't afford something, it means you don't or you won't have enough money to buy
it.
Aaron says that Vance deserves a raise because he's got a great track record with the company.
A great track record means a great history of performance.
And Vance has also put in overtime when needed.
Overtime refers to working more than the normal hours.
However, the supervisor, Mr. Brown, is always fussing about how they need to cut costs.
The verb fussing means complaining.
Aaron agrees that Mr. Brown definitely doesn't tolerate any nonsense, but he suggests that
that's for the best, because he respects men who are up front and straight forward.
Up front means direct.
Mr. Brown doesn't like weaklings.
The word weakling is an informal word for someone who is weak, or who doesn't have much
courage.
Aaron advises Vance, if you go into his office hanging your head and beating around the
bush, he's just going to kick you out.
Hanging your head means having your head down, looking down at the floor, as if you were
ashamed.
And beating around the bush means saying things that are somewhat related, but not getting
to the main point.
So, Aaron says if you do this, if you go into his office hanging your head and beating around
the bush, he's just going to kick you out.
To kick someone out means to expel the person, put the person out by force.
Instead, Aaron recommends, you have to march into that man's office with your chin up, look
him in the eye and ask with confidence.
The verb march means to walk confidently.
We also use march when talking about soldiers walking or marching, together in an army.
Aaron has asked Mr. Brown for a raise in the past.
When he did so, at first Mr. Brown yelled at him and threw a lot of financial numbers
around and so on.
And so on means and more of this type of thing.
But Aaron held his ground.
To hold your ground means to maintain your position and not give up or give in.
The reason Aaron asked for a raise was because his twins were about to go to college, with
a double tuition bill to boot.
To boot is an informal way to say in addition, something that makes a situation even worse
or even better, even more intense.
So that's why Aaron needed a raise and he got one.
Vance says, I can't believe you pulled that off.
To pull something off means to manage to succeed in doing something difficult.
Aaron says, look, Mr. Brown isn't blind.
If you say someone isn't blind, it means they are not unaware of what's happening.
In other words, they are aware, they understand and see what is happening.
He knows the cost of living is going up.
He also knows we give it our all.
If you give something your all, it means you give it your best effort and energy.
Currently Vance and Melinda are living in a small apartment and when the baby arrives, space
will be very tight.
In this context, the word tight means small and uncomfortable.
So Aaron encourages Vance to just tell Mr. Brown the truth.
Aaron thinks that Mr. Brown is a reasonable man.
He says, sure, he might bark at you, but don't back down.
To bark at someone means to speak harshly to the person.
And don't back down means don't change your position or belief.
Stay strong in the middle of a conflict or disagreement with another person.
Vance hopes he doesn't catch Mr. Brown on a bad day, saying, I can just picture getting
fired with the baby on the way.
I can just picture means I can just imagine.
The word picture when used as a verb means imagine, make a mental picture of a thing or
a situation.
Aaron encourages Vance not to delay and to go see Mr. Brown now.
Vance says, well, here goes.
Here goes is an expression when the speaker is about to perform a bold, risky or difficult
action.
And Aaron says, don't be surprised if Mr. Brown melts a little.
In this context, the word melt refers to becoming less hard and showing more emotion.
Don't be surprised if Mr. Brown melts a little and buys you a housewarming present.
A housewarming present is a gift to celebrate moving into a new house.
Sometimes when people, especially married couples, move into a new house, they have a
housewarming party, which celebrates the move into the new house.
And people might give them presents, such as small appliances and other things for the
house.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.

speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
